```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "The additive trend as published, and the same trend with the four beetle by fire product terms added. Intervals are the naive Poisson intervals the published likelihood implies, and terms excluding zero on those intervals are marked. Read this way the interaction is emphatic; @sec-pphonest reads it the other way."

## pois_ci and SE_ADD are defined in sec-ppreproduce, where the reproduction of
## the published standard errors needs them.
SE_PROD <- pois_ci(X_PROD, B_PROD)

side <- function(b, se, lbl) tibble(
  Term = names(b), Model = lbl, Estimate = round(unname(b), 3),
  Interval = ci_txt(b - 1.96 * se, b + 1.96 * se),
  ` ` = ifelse(clears(b - 1.96 * se, b + 1.96 * se), "excludes zero", ""))
PRODT <- grep(":", names(B_PROD), value = TRUE)
PROD <- bind_rows(side(B_ADD, SE_ADD, "As published"),
                  side(B_PROD, SE_PROD, "With product terms")) |>
  filter(Term != "(Intercept)")

## The likelihood ratio the published likelihood would report.
dev_of <- function(X, b) {
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b)) * PP$w; y <- PP$yy * PP$w
  2 * sum(ifelse(y > 0, y * log(y / mu), 0) - (y - mu))
}
LR_STAT <- dev_of(X_ADD, B_ADD) - dev_of(X_PROD, B_PROD)
LR_DF   <- length(PRODT)
LR_P    <- pchisq(LR_STAT, LR_DF, lower.tail = FALSE)
N_PROD_SIG <- sum(clears(B_PROD[PRODT] - 1.96 * SE_PROD[PRODT],
                         B_PROD[PRODT] + 1.96 * SE_PROD[PRODT]))
show(PROD, "tbl-ppproduct", "llrll") |> collapse_rows(2, valign = "top")
```

Read through the likelihood the published model is fitted with, the interaction is not marginal. The likelihood ratio statistic is `r sprintf("%.1f", LR_STAT)` on `r LR_DF` degrees of freedom, a p-value below `r format(signif(max(LR_P, 1e-16), 1), scientific = TRUE)`, and `r N_PROD_SIG` of the `r LR_DF` product terms carry intervals excluding zero. An analyst who stopped here would report that the compound-disturbance interaction is confirmed, and would have the parent study's own machinery behind the claim.

Two details ought to give pause before that is written down. The product terms do not share a sign: grey attack raises regeneration at high severity and lowers it at low severity, and the fitted signs reverse between the two beetle surfaces on the same severity class. And adding them moves the main effects sharply, taking the high-severity term from `r sprintf("%.3f", B_ADD[["Fire_H"]])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", B_PROD[["Fire_H"]])`. A product term that is real usually leaves the rest of the model roughly where it found it.

## Spatially adjusted inference {#sec-pphonest}

The published fit is described as an inhomogeneous log-Gaussian Cox process, and estimating the trend of a Cox process by the Berman-Turner device is legitimate: the Poisson score is a composite likelihood, and it returns consistent estimates of the trend whether or not the process is Poisson [@baddeley2000; @waagepetersen2007]. What the composite likelihood does not return is the variance. The standard errors it reports are the standard errors of the Poisson model it is arithmetically equivalent to, and those assume seedlings are placed independently given the covariates. So the estimates carry the Cox specification and the uncertainty carries the Poisson one, and only the second is affected.

That the process is not Poisson is established in the parent study itself. It devotes two figures to Ripley's inhomogeneous K, testing the observed pattern against a null of non-constant intensity through 999 Monte Carlo simulations, and reports significant clustering for every species examined [@murphy2026]. Conifer regeneration is clustered, for seed-dispersal and microsite reasons that have nothing to do with the covariates, and finding it so is the expected result rather than a defect. The point is only that the same paper cannot use a clustered-process diagnostic as a result and an independent-process variance as its inference. The residuals of the refit say the same thing directly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlogram
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Residual dependence at the two scales the study works at. Left, the conditioned model of @sec-conditioning across the burn, where dependence has largely decayed by 500 m. Right, the fit with product terms over the quadrature points inside the regeneration plots, where it has decayed by about 100 m. The two panels are the same obstacle two orders of magnitude apart, and each sets the block sizes tried at its own scale."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 3.2

pres <- function(X, b) {
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b)) * PP$w
  (PP$yy * PP$w - mu) / sqrt(mu)
}
rq <- pres(X_PROD, B_PROD)[!PP$data_pt]
rq <- rq - mean(rq)
set.seed(7)
jj <- sample(nrow(Q), min(2500L, nrow(Q)))
dd <- as.vector(dist(cbind(Q$x[jj], Q$y[jj])))
rr <- outer(rq[jj], rq[jj]) / mean(rq[jj]^2)
rr <- rr[lower.tri(rr)]
pbins <- cut(dd, c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, Inf))
PCORR <- tibble(`Lag (m)` = levels(pbins),
                `Residual correlation` = round(as.numeric(tapply(rr, pbins, mean)), 3)) |>
  filter(!is.na(`Residual correlation`))
invisible(keep(PCORR, "fig-correlogram"))

## Bin midpoints for plotting. cut() labels are "(a,b]", and the open final bin
## has no midpoint, so it is dropped rather than given an invented one.
mid_of <- function(lab) {
  n <- regmatches(lab, gregexpr("-?[0-9.]+|Inf", lab))
  vapply(n, function(v) mean(as.numeric(v)), numeric(1))
}
corr_df <- function(x, scale) {
  x |> mutate(Lag = mid_of(`Lag (m)`), Scale = scale) |>
    filter(is.finite(Lag)) |> select(Lag, r = `Residual correlation`, Scale)
}
CORR_BOTH <- bind_rows(
  corr_df(CORR,  "Across the burn, conditioned model"),
  corr_df(PCORR, "Inside the plots, fit with product terms"))

FIG_CORR <- ggplot(CORR_BOTH, aes(Lag, r)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "22", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, colour = "#7b3294") +
  geom_point(size = 1.9, colour = "#7b3294") +
  facet_wrap(~ Scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Lag (m)", y = "Residual correlation") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8))
CORR_PATH <- file.path("..", "03.outputs", "PNG", "fig-correlogram.png")
ggsave(CORR_PATH, FIG_CORR, width = 7.2, height = 3.2, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(CORR_PATH)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppcorr
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Residual correlogram of the fit with product terms, over the quadrature points inside the plots. This is the right panel of @fig-correlogram at the precision that sets the block sizes tried below."

show(PCORR, "tbl-ppcorr", "lr")
```

Dependence runs at `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[1]` inside 25 m and is still `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[3]` between 50 and 75 m, crossing zero at around 100 m (@tbl-ppcorr). A block that contains it must therefore be at least 75 to 100 m on a side, and a 200 m plot affords few of those. That collision is the same one @sec-blocks met at landscape scale, arriving again two orders of magnitude down.

```{r}
#| label: fig-interaction
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The four product terms and the main effects they modify, under the Poisson likelihood the published model is fitted with and under a spatial block bootstrap across block sizes spanning the residual range. The estimate is the same in every case; only the interval changes. Three of the four product terms exclude zero under the Poisson likelihood and none excludes it at any block size."
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.4

pp_boot <- function(X, side_m, seed = 11) {
  ids <- split(seq_len(nrow(PP)), paste(PP$x %/% side_m, PP$y %/% side_m))
  K <- length(ids)
  set.seed(seed)
  M <- vapply(seq_len(B_BOOT),
              function(b) pfit(X, unlist(ids[sample.int(K, K, TRUE)], use.names = FALSE)),
              numeric(ncol(X)))
  ci <- apply(M, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Term = colnames(X), Lower = ci[1, ], Upper = ci[2, ], K = K,
         Usable = apply(M, 1, function(v) sum(is.finite(v))))
}

PP_SHOWN <- c("MPB_G", "MPB_R", "Fire_H", "Fire_L", PRODT)
PPB_RAW <- bind_rows(lapply(PP_SWEEP, function(m)
  pp_boot(X_PROD, m) |> filter(Term %in% PP_SHOWN) |> mutate(`Block side (m)` = m)))

## The ground each product term is estimated from: quadrature points where both
## of its indicators are on. This is what a resample has to miss for the term to
## become unidentified, so it is the number that explains the Usable counts.
PROD_CELLS <- vapply(PRODT, function(t) {
  v <- strsplit(t, ":", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  sum(Q[[v[1]]] == 1 & Q[[v[2]]] == 1)
}, integer(1))

## Identification, carried forward rather than averaged away. A term is fully
## identified at a block size only if every one of the B_BOOT draws estimated it;
## anything less means some resample omitted the blocks carrying its cells, and
## the percentile for that term is then taken over a selected subset of draws.
PPB_RAW <- PPB_RAW |> mutate(Identified = Usable == B_BOOT)

PPB <- PPB_RAW |>
  transmute(`Block side (m)`, Blocks = K, Term,
            Estimate = round(B_PROD[Term], 3),
            Interval = ci_txt(Lower, Upper),
            `Draws` = paste0(Usable, "/", B_BOOT),
            ` ` = ifelse(clears(Lower, Upper), "clears zero", "spans zero"))
invisible(keep(PPB, "fig-interaction"))

## The published likelihood's own interval, drawn beside the block intervals so
## the comparison the paper rests on is one figure rather than two tables.
## Design-matrix column names are not axis labels. Written once here and reused
## by the verdict chunk below, so the figure and the prose cannot disagree.
PP_WORDS <- c(MPB_G = "grey attack", MPB_R = "red attack",
              Fire_H = "high severity", Fire_L = "low severity")
pp_label <- function(term) {
  parts <- strsplit(term, ":", fixed = TRUE)
  vapply(parts, function(v) {
    lab <- paste(PP_WORDS[v], collapse = " by ")
    paste0(toupper(substring(lab, 1, 1)), substring(lab, 2))
  }, character(1))
}

SRC <- c("Poisson likelihood", paste(PP_SWEEP, "m blocks"))
PPF <- bind_rows(
  tibble(Term = PP_SHOWN, Lower = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] - 1.96 * SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN],
         Upper = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] + 1.96 * SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN], Source = SRC[1]),
  PPB_RAW |> transmute(Term, Lower, Upper,
                       Source = paste(`Block side (m)`, "m blocks"))) |>
  mutate(Estimate = B_PROD[Term],
         Source = factor(Source, levels = SRC),
         Kind = factor(ifelse(grepl(":", Term), "Product terms", "Main effects"),
                       levels = c("Main effects", "Product terms")),
         Term = factor(pp_label(Term), levels = rev(pp_label(PP_SHOWN))))

FIG_INT <- ggplot(PPF, aes(Estimate, Term, colour = Source)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "22", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = Lower, xmax = Upper),
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), size = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#c6dbef", "#6baed6", "#2171b5", "#08306b"),
                      name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(Kind ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1, reverse = FALSE)) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8, angle = -90))
INT_PATH <- file.path("..", "03.outputs", "PNG", "fig-interaction.png")
ggsave(INT_PATH, FIG_INT, width = 7.4, height = 4.4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
knitr::include_graphics(INT_PATH)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppblocks
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The same intervals as numbers, with the count of bootstrap draws that identified each term. A term short of the full count was unestimable in some resample, because the blocks carrying its cells were not drawn; its interval is then a percentile over the draws that did identify it and is read accordingly."

show(PPB, "tbl-ppblocks", "rrlrlrl") |> collapse_rows(1:2, valign = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sandwich
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "A second variance estimate, independent of the bootstrap. Standard errors for the fit with product terms under the naive Poisson likelihood and under a cluster-robust sandwich clustered on the same spatial blocks, with the ratio between them. The bootstrap resamples blocks; the sandwich sums scores within them. The two answer the same question by different routes."

## A block bootstrap over 14 to 36 blocks sits below the percentile method's
## comfortable floor, so the inference should not rest on it alone. The sandwich
## is the check a referee will already trust: the bread is the same Poisson
## information pois_ci inverts, and the meat is the outer product of scores
## summed within block, so dependence inside a block is carried and dependence
## between blocks is assumed away. Same assumption as the bootstrap, different
## estimator.
cluster_se <- function(X, b, side_m) {
  mu <- exp(drop(X %*% b))
  V  <- solve(crossprod(X, X * (mu * PP$w)))          # bread: Poisson information
  U  <- (PP$w * (PP$yy - mu)) * X                     # score contribution per point
  S  <- rowsum(U, paste(PP$x %/% side_m, PP$y %/% side_m))
  G  <- nrow(S)
  ## The usual finite-cluster correction. With G this small it is not cosmetic.
  meat <- crossprod(S) * (G / (G - 1))
  sqrt(diag(V %*% meat %*% V))
}

SAND <- bind_rows(lapply(PP_OK, function(m) {
  se <- cluster_se(X_PROD, B_PROD, m)
  tibble(`Block side (m)` = m, Term = PP_SHOWN,
         `Poisson SE` = round(unname(SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN]), 3),
         `Cluster-robust SE` = round(unname(se[PP_SHOWN]), 3),
         Ratio = round(unname(se[PP_SHOWN] / SE_PROD[PP_SHOWN]), 1),
         lo = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] - 1.96 * se[PP_SHOWN],
         hi = B_PROD[PP_SHOWN] + 1.96 * se[PP_SHOWN])
}))

## The same verdict the bootstrap was asked for, from the other estimator.
SAND_PROD_CLEAR <- sum(clears(SAND$lo[SAND$Term %in% PRODT],
                              SAND$hi[SAND$Term %in% PRODT]))
SAND_N_PROD <- sum(SAND$Term %in% PRODT)
SAND_RANGE  <- range(SAND$Ratio)

show(SAND |> select(-lo, -hi) |>
       mutate(Term = pp_label(Term)), "tbl-sandwich", "rlrrr") |>
  collapse_rows(1, valign = "top")
```

The sandwich of @tbl-sandwich agrees with the bootstrap of @tbl-ppblocks on both counts. It inflates the standard errors by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", SAND_RANGE[1])` to `r sprintf("%.1f", SAND_RANGE[2])`, in the same range as the interval widening the resampling produces, and of the `r SAND_N_PROD` product-term intervals it implies across the block sizes the correlogram licenses, `r SAND_PROD_CLEAR` exclude zero. Two estimators that share an assumption are not independent evidence, and both assume that blocks are independent of one another. But they differ in everything else, and a result that survived one because of an artefact of the other's construction would not survive both.

**The direction of the remaining error is worth stating, because it does not run the same way for the two results.** Any residual dependence these methods fail to capture leaves the intervals still too narrow. For the product terms that is a conservative failure: the intervals reported here are, if anything, narrower than they should be, and they already span zero, so a fuller accounting of dependence can only strengthen the conclusion that the interaction is unsupported. For the moderate-severity peak of @sec-conditioning it runs the other way. That result is positive, it rests on an interval excluding zero, and an interval that is too narrow is exactly what would manufacture it. The negative result here is therefore the more secure of the two, and the positive one is reported at @sec-blocks with its weakest block size named for that reason.

```{r}
#| label: pp-verdict
#| echo: true
#| output: false

## Let the sweep state the conclusion. Asserting one that a refit could
## invalidate is the error sec-blocks records having made once already.
PROD_ROWS  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(Term %in% PRODT)
PROD_CLEAR <- sum(clears(PROD_ROWS$Lower, PROD_ROWS$Upper))

MAIN_KEEP  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(!Term %in% PRODT) |>
  group_by(Term) |> summarise(all_clear = all(clears(Lower, Upper)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(all_clear) |> pull(Term)
MAIN_WORDS <- paste(tolower(pp_label(MAIN_KEEP)), collapse = " and ")

## PP_OK, the block sizes the correlogram licenses, is declared in setup because
## tbl-sandwich needs it upstream of here.
PP_OK_K  <- PPB_RAW |> filter(`Block side (m)` %in% PP_OK) |>
  distinct(`Block side (m)`, K) |> arrange(desc(K))
PP_OK_TXT <- paste(sprintf("%d at %d m", PP_OK_K$K, PP_OK_K$`Block side (m)`),
                   collapse = " and ")
## The widening factor is the paper's headline number, so it is computed only
## where every draw identified the term. A partially identified term has an
## interval taken over a selected subset of resamples, which inflates it for a
## reason that has nothing to do with spatial dependence, and quoting that as
## the cost of honest inference would overstate the case.
DEGEN <- PPB_RAW |> filter(!Identified)
WIDEN <- PPB_RAW |> filter(Identified) |>
  mutate(naive = 2 * 1.96 * SE_PROD[Term], ratio = (Upper - Lower) / naive) |>
  summarise(lo = min(ratio), hi = max(ratio), n = n())

## The abstract lives in the YAML, where an inline `r` expression does not run, so
## its six quantities are the only hard-coded numbers in the document. They are
## asserted here instead: a refit that moves any of them fails the render rather
## than leaving the abstract quietly contradicting the results.
## This guard is only real with `error: false` in the YAML. Under `error: true`
## a failure here printed nothing at all, because the chunk also sets
## `output: false`, and the render exited 0 with the abstract contradicting the
## results. That is how the previous 2.4 and 7.6 survived a refit that moved
## them. Do not set `error: true`, and do not remove `output: false` in place of
## fixing it, because the chunk's console noise is not the point of it.
stopifnot(sprintf("%.3f", MOD_ADJ) == "0.416",
          sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo) == "2.3",
          sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi) == "5.9",
          nrow(PROD_ROWS) == 16,
          PROD_CLEAR == 0,
          SAND_PROD_CLEAR == 0)
```

**Not one of the `r nrow(PROD_ROWS)` product-term intervals excludes zero.** Across four block sizes and `r LR_DF` product terms the count that clears is `r PROD_CLEAR`. The estimates have not moved, because the estimates are not what was wrong; the intervals have widened by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)` against the naive Poisson intervals of @tbl-ppproduct, and that factor is the whole of the difference between an interaction that looks overwhelming and one that is not there.

That factor is quoted only over the `r WIDEN$n` of `r nrow(PPB_RAW)` term-by-block combinations that every one of the `r format(B_BOOT, big.mark = ",")` draws could estimate, and the reason is worth recording because it is the same kind of fault the paper is about. The four product cells rest on `r min(PROD_CELLS)` to `r max(PROD_CELLS)` quadrature points each, so a resample that misses the blocks holding one of them leaves that term unidentified. `r nrow(DEGEN)` combinations were affected, every one of them involving red attack or high severity, the worst losing `r B_BOOT - min(PPB_RAW$Usable)` draws of `r format(B_BOOT, big.mark = ",")`. The percentile for such a term is taken over whichever resamples happened to contain its cells, which are the resamples that overweight them, and that inflates the interval for a reason having nothing to do with spatial dependence. Left in, those combinations put the top of the widening range at `r sprintf("%.1f", max((PPB_RAW$Upper - PPB_RAW$Lower) / (2 * 1.96 * SE_PROD[PPB_RAW$Term])))` rather than `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`. The count of usable draws is reported in @tbl-ppblocks for every cell so that this is visible rather than averaged away, and none of it changes the verdict: the affected intervals were already the widest, and every product term spans zero on the identified combinations alone.

What survives is thin and worth stating precisely. The only terms among those shown whose intervals exclude zero at every block size are `r MAIN_WORDS`. Neither is a product term. The regeneration data support main effects for red-stage beetle attack and low burn severity, and support no statement at all about the two agents acting together.

This is not a demonstration that the agents do not interact. It is a demonstration that these data cannot tell. Three plots totalling `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha afford `r PP_OK_TXT` across the block sizes the residual range permits, and a product term asks the data to resolve a difference of differences across four severity-by-attack combinations on that footprint. The published likelihood answers the question confidently because it counts `r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` seedlings as `r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` independent pieces of evidence. They are not.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Two questions were asked. Neither returned the answer it was posed to find, and the reasons are different in kind.

## Principal findings {#sec-found}

**Beetle and fire cannot be compared across the fire perimeter here, because the surfaces that would do it stop at the perimeter.** The annual classifications from which every local beetle surface descends carry nodata across almost all of the unburned forest, and carried it before any classification that used them was run. The consequence is not a caveat: a contingency table built across the boundary reports attack rising from a fraction of a per cent in unburned forest to a fifth at moderate severity, and measures the mask. The provincial Aerial Overview Survey, never clipped, finds attack outside the perimeter at a rate no lower than inside it.

**Within the burn the severity gradient is real and narrow.** Three records that do not share a measurement pathway agree that attack peaks at moderate severity, and conditioning on lodgepole cover and elevation attenuates that peak by about two fifths without removing it. The fall at high severity is not supported in any specification, so the non-monotone shape is a claim these data carry at its peak and not at its fall.

**The beetle by fire interaction is not supported.** Through the likelihood the parent study uses it is emphatic: a likelihood ratio statistic of `r sprintf("%.1f", LR_STAT)` on `r LR_DF` degrees of freedom and `r N_PROD_SIG` of `r LR_DF` product terms excluding zero. Under inference accounting for the clustering of the seedling pattern, every product term spans zero at every block size tried, and a cluster-robust sandwich clustered on the same blocks agrees. The estimates do not move; only the intervals do, by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`, and that factor is the whole distance between a confirmed interaction and none.

## Inferential generality {#sec-general}

The parent study reports that "areas of overlapping beetle mortality and high burn severity had significantly reduced lodgepole pine regeneration" and reads from that the suggestion that "the ecological consequences of beetle-fire interactions weaken as surface fuels decay over time". Its specification enters the two agents additively and tests no product between them. This paper adds one and finds that the data cannot support it either way, which means the additive specification was the right one to have fitted. The finding is therefore not a revision of the parent's ecology. It is a statement about what these data can be asked, and it locates the limit in the inference rather than in the landscape.

The mechanism is worth stating plainly, because it is not specific to this landscape. A point process trend fitted by the Berman-Turner device is a weighted Poisson regression [@berman1992; @baddeley2000], and a Poisson likelihood treats every seedling as an independent piece of evidence about the covariates. The parent study devotes two figures and 999 Monte Carlo simulations to establishing that the seedling pattern is not independent: it reports significant clustering in every species examined, which is the expected result for conifer regeneration and not a defect [@murphy2026]. Those two facts sit in the same paper, and the second invalidates the standard errors the first is reported alongside. The residual correlogram of @fig-correlogram reaches the same verdict from inside the model, with dependence of `r PCORR$"Residual correlation"[1]` within 25 m.

This is not an unusual error and it is not a careless one: clustered point patterns are routinely fitted this way and the software makes the Poisson path the path of least resistance. What makes it consequential is the size of the correction. A misspecified likelihood does not usually move a coefficient, it moves the interval around it, and the interval is what the claim rests on.

**The caution this implies is not new, and the more careful practice already exists.** Modelling conifer regeneration after a large mixed-severity fire, @donato2009 excluded from their candidate set any model carrying more than five predictors or any interaction term, on the stated ground that the sample was too modest to support them, and reported relative importance among additive predictors instead. That is a judgement made in advance, on a study of comparable design and larger extent, and it reaches by prior reasoning the conclusion this paper reaches by measurement. The two routes are worth having both of. A restraint exercised on principle is cheap but unquantified, and leaves open how much room the data would in fact have allowed; a restraint arrived at by measurement puts a number on it, and that number is what transfers to the next study. The result reported here is therefore a quantification of a discipline this literature already exercises, not an objection to anyone who failed to.

## Extent constraints {#sec-extent}

Every result here is bounded by an extent chosen by a disturbance rather than by a design. The burn is about eight square kilometres and the regeneration plots total `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha inside it: the ground on which beetle and fire co-occur at all, so not an arbitrary choice, but not a neutral one either.

The consequences run the same way at both scales. Across the burn, lodgepole cover and elevation correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", R_PL_EL)` and cannot be separated, where the companion study distinguishes them because 1,776 m of relief contains pine-poor ground at every height [@murphy2026refugia]. The fitted elevation optimum lands at `r round(PEAK)` m, far below the range the clip spans, so an analyst working only here would report attack rising with elevation without limit; the landscape-scale hump is not contradicted but out of view.

The same collision governs the inference. A block bootstrap needs blocks large enough to contain the dependence and numerous enough to resample, and at both scales the extent caps the first before the second is comfortable: a 500 m block holds most of the dependence across the burn and affords `r SWEEP$Blocks[SWEEP$"Block side (m)" == BLOCK_M]`, where 1 km would afford eight, and inside the plots the residual range demands 75 to 100 m and the plots afford `r PP_OK_TXT`. This is the paper's subject matter arriving in its own methods: the extent that makes a compound-disturbance question askable is the extent that decides how firmly it can be answered.

## Limitations {#sec-limits}

Four of this study's five results are negative, and they are reported at the same length and in the same register as the one that is not. That is a deliberate choice rather than an apology. The same practice is visible in recent work on burn severity in this literature: @estabrook2025 report a severity model with acceptable discrimination and then state plainly that the map built from it performed poorly, with a residual spatial structure their own diagnostic detected. A negative applied result reported clearly is more useful than a positive one reported without its diagnostics, and the limitations below are set out in that spirit.

**The interaction result is a null, and nulls have a floor.** Nothing here shows that beetle mortality and burn severity do not interact. It shows that `r format(N_DATA, big.mark = ",")` seedlings across `r sprintf("%.1f", WIN_HA)` ha, clustered as this pattern is, cannot resolve a difference of differences across four severity-by-attack combinations. A larger or better distributed sample could return a different answer, and this study offers no estimate of how much larger.

**Question A is answered in a reduced form.** The within-burn gradient is not the question the compound-disturbance literature asks, which is whether beetle-killed stands burn differently from stands that were not attacked. Recovering that comparison means rebuilding the classification over the unclipped landscape, a reprocessing task that re-treads the parent study's published methods.

**Two beetle surfaces disagree and only one is documented.** The corrected grey-stage union is preferred throughout: three times denser than the published red-stage surface, observed throughout the perimeter, and derived by a script that survives [@murphy2026greyfix]. The red-stage surface is a substitution for a layer absent from the parent repository and searched for without success.

**The severity reference category is inherited, not chosen.** The published specification carries indicators for high and low severity only, so moderate severity is pooled with unburned and unclassified ground into a reference that is `r round(100 * REF_MOD / REF_N)` per cent moderate, the class carrying the most beetle attack. It is reproduced rather than repaired, because the object was to test the published model rather than replace it, but no fire coefficient here means quite what its label says.

**The provincial survey is a coarse instrument**, its polygons sketched from an aircraft at a mapping scale far coarser than 30 m. It is used only as a check on whether ground outside the perimeter carries attack at all, which it can answer, and not as a measurement of severity, which it cannot.

## Research priorities {#sec-next}

Three things, in descending order of value against cost. The interaction test should be repeated where extent is not the binding constraint, which given the dependence range measured here means a distributed plot network rather than three contiguous plots. The published point process results should be reported with intervals that respect the clustering, which is inexpensive because the estimates are unchanged, and which on the evidence of @fig-interaction leaves two main effects standing. And recovering question A in its original form requires rebuilding the beetle classification over the unclipped landscape, which is worth doing only if the Landsat archive is being revisited anyway.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

Compound disturbance is described as an interaction far more often than it is tested as one, and the gap between the description and the test is where this study lives.

Three findings, stated at the confidence the data support.

1.  **A provenance result.** The beetle surfaces underlying the parent study stop at the fire perimeter, in the source files, before classification. Any comparison of beetle attack across that boundary measures the clip and not the forest. This is checkable in any study that inherits rasters it did not build, and it is cheap to check.

2.  **A narrow ecological result.** Inside the burn, beetle attack is elevated at moderate severity relative to low, by `r sprintf("%.3f", MOD_ADJ)` in log-odds after conditioning on host and elevation, and it clears a spatial block bootstrap interval at every block size the extent supports. Attack at high severity is not distinguishable from attack at low severity in any specification.

3.  **A negative result about the interaction, and a positive one about why.** The beetle by fire product term is decisive under the published Poisson likelihood and absent under inference that accounts for the clustering the parent study itself documents. The coefficients are identical either way. Only the intervals differ, and they differ by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", WIDEN$hi)`.

The title of this paper is a description of the parent study and, on this evidence, a recommendation. Beetle and fire were modelled additively there. Nothing found here supports modelling them any other way with data of this extent, and the apparent support for doing so came from a likelihood that counted clustered seedlings as independent observations. The honest summary of a compound-disturbance interaction in this landscape is that it has not been demonstrated, that these data cannot demonstrate it, and that the confidence with which it can appear to have been demonstrated is the finding most worth carrying elsewhere.
